title: How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days
full_review:
A guy takes a bet he can make a particular woman quickly fall in love with him, unaware she's targeted him as the subject of a magazine article, "How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days" (Paramount).

If the set-up sounds strained, just imagine almost two hours of watching it unfold, in full-throttle cutesy mode.

Kate Hudson's Andie is a beauty magazine columnist, wanting to write serious political stories. But her boss (Bebe Neuwirth) likes the idea of an article on all the wrong things to do that would drive a man away -- and Andie's got the assignment.

Ad exec Barry (Matthew McConaughey) wants to head the campaign for a diamond client but his boss (a bland Robert Klein) is dubious. To convince him, Barry boasts he can make any woman fall in love with him. The two women also competing for the diamond account know of Andie's assignment, so tell him Andie's the one he must woo and win.

Easily smitten by the vivacious blonde, he's puzzled after a few days when she starts filling his bathroom shelves with her cosmetics, adding stuffed animals to his decor and showing up at his office with awful shirts she insists he wear immediately. But when she barges in on his poker night with his buddies and makes him blow his nose on her command, he tells her off -- only to apologize and make up later, to her dismay. Can he put up with her possessiveness by day 10?

Yes, Kate Hudson can be adorable, but the script has her flirting and batting her eyelashes with such abandon that she wears you out. Proceeding day-by-day to the climactic 10th day, director Donald Petrie's movie makes one wish the time frame was half as long; it might have made the drawn-out movie flow twice as well.

McConaughey starts looking uncomfortable in the role once Andie shows her spoiled brat and clingy side that severely tests his resolve. He's hard pressed to be convincing from then on and the lack of sparkling dialogue in a romantic comedy is especially noticeable. The crucial scene at the diamond client's party, where each learns the other's real intentions, rings false, only to lead into the expected resolution.

Surprisingly, the movie is not really about getting them into bed, although eventually that is implied after she spends a weekend with his down-to-earth family on Staten Island.

With its pert New York City settings and an attractive-looking cast, it may please the undemanding, but it's no loss to a guy or gal to lose this flick.

Due to sexual references, fleeting violence, some rude slang expressions and occasional profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Office for Film and Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13
